name: Devanatha Perumal Temple, Thiruvahindrapuram
deity: Vishnu as Devanatha Perumal, standing, with the Goddess Hemambujavalli (Vaikuntanayaki); the festival image is Moovaragiya Oruvan, 'the One who is the Three'
period: A Divya Desam of Nadu Nadu on the Kedilam river, sung by Thirumangai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
dynasty: Medieval Chola, with later Pandya additions
summary: Beside the Kedilam near Cuddalore, Vishnu stands as Devanatha Perumal, lord of the gods — a Divya Desam sung by Thirumangai Alvar, and the town where Vedanta Desika lived, worshipped and received Hayagriva.

sections.history: Thiruvahindrapuram, near Cuddalore on the banks of the Kedilam, is one of the 108 Divya Desams and belongs to Nadu Nadu, the 'middle country' between the Chola and Pallava lands. Thirumangai Alvar sang ten verses on its lord in the Periya Thirumozhi, hailing Devanatha as the one godhead who is Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva together. The temple is held to have been built under the Medieval Cholas and enlarged by the Pandyas. Inscriptions of Rajaraja I on the ardhamandapa name the place Thiru-ayindapuram and record a village given to the temple, and an eleventh-century record notes a land gift by his chief queen, Trilokamadevi. The town is dear to Sri Vaishnavas above all as the home of Vedanta Desika, who spent some of the most eventful years of his life here; his house and the well he dug still stand.
sections.architecture: A five-tiered rajagopuram, about eighteen metres high, opens on three prakarams around the east-facing sanctum. The vimana above it is likened to the Suddha Satva vimana of Vaikuntha and bears figures facing the four quarters — Vishnu to the east, Dakshinamurthy to the south, Narasimha to the west and Brahma to the north. The Goddess Hemambujavalli has her own shrine. Beside the temple rises the small Aushadagiri hill, crowned by a shrine to Hayagriva, said to be the only historic hilltop Hayagriva shrine in South India.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Adisesha, the serpent on whom Vishnu rests, planned and founded this town — hence Ahindrapuram, the city of the serpent-lord. Once, when the Lord thirsted, Garuda ploughed the earth with his beak to bring a stream, while Adisesha cut his own channel and returned first; the Lord drank from Adisesha's water. To console Garuda, it is said, the Lord's ritual bath is still drawn from Garuda's stream and his offerings from the Sesha Theertham. Tradition holds that on the Aushadagiri Vedanta Desika worshipped Garuda and received the grace of Hayagriva.
sections.festivals: The ten-day Brahmotsavam in Chittirai (April–May) is the high point, with Garuda Seva on the fifth day and the Theerthavari on the ninth drawing great crowds. Vedanta Desika's birth-star is celebrated in Purattasi. Vaikunta Ekadashi, Adi Pooram and the Masi Magam sea bath at Devanampattinam complete the year.
sections.experience: Come for darshan of Devanatha, then climb the steps of the Aushadagiri to the Hayagriva shrine, a place students visit to pray for learning. In the village, ask for Desikan Tirumaligai, the house of Vedanta Desika, and his well. Mornings beside the Kedilam are quiet and unhurried, a contrast to the festival crowds of Chittirai.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; Brahmotsavam days, Vaikunta Ekadashi and weekends are busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is a short drive from Cuddalore town, which has railway stations and road links along the East Coast Road; Puducherry lies about an hour north, and Chennai has the nearest major airport.
